title: Humble before truth
hookLine: the dialogue ends with the yogis honoring the Word

cards: An old balance scale: two pans hanging from a beam. Put something on each side and watch. One pan rises, the other sinks, and the one that sinks has more in it.

Guru Nanak used that scale. The Siddhs in the Sidh Gosht were people of standing, masters of hard disciplines, used to being the ones others came to. The dialogue is long, and the questions are sharp.
So how does a meeting like that end, between people who don't bend easily?

teach.h: THE HONOR GOES TO THE WORD.
teach.b: First, the ending. It's told in more than one place. The Sidh Gosht itself closes on the Word: in paraphrase, without the True Word there is no freedom, and the Gurmukh is the one who finds it.

Bhai Gurdas, the early Sikh poet whose Vaars are read alongside scripture, tells of Nanak meeting the Siddhs, and in his telling they end by praising the work of Nanak's life, a life spent pointing to the Name.
Read together, the honor doesn't land on a debating score. It lands on the truth being talked about, and on a life that lived it. Now the scale.
In the Asa di Var, Guru Nanak has a short verse about bowing. In paraphrase: everyone bows to themselves; no one bows to another.

teach.h: THE SIDE THAT BOWS IS HEAVIER.
teach.b: Put things on a balance and weigh them: the side that bows is the heavier one. We usually think the one who stays upright is strong and the one who bends is weak. The verse turns it over.
Bowing shows weight; the empty pan floats up.
Right beside that verse, the Asa di Var gives two words that sum it up, mithat neevee: sweetness and humility, the essence of virtue and goodness.
So when the yogis bow, it isn't a defeat on a scoreboard.

Masters of their craft, they still had room to honor something true from outside their own order. That's heavy. And at the start of the dialogue, before a single argument, Nanak's first move was a bow to the True One.
Humility runs both ways across that mountain.

how: Sikhs bow before the Guru Granth Sahib on entering a gurdwara, touching the forehead to the floor, and the Asa di Var, with its verse on sweetness and humility, is sung in gurdwaras in the early morning.

o: giving in to whoever argues the loudest
honoring truth, even from outside your own circle
staying silent so nobody's feelings get hurt

games.q: what's inside humble before truth — tap the pairs.
p: goes to the Word, not a winner
early Sikh poet of the Vaars

s: in Guru Nanak's verse, the pan that rises is the weightier one
the side that bows is the heavier one.
the honor at the end goes to the Word, not to the cleverest speaker
the dialogue pointed to the True Word all along.
humility in the Sidh Gosht runs only one way
the dialogue opens with greetings, and with Nanak bowing to the True One before any argument.

games.q: two pans on a balance. one rises, one sinks. which does Guru Nanak's verse compare to the person who bows?
o: the pan that rises: light and free.
the pan that sinks: the heavier one.
neither: the beam in the middle.
games.why: weigh them on a balance, the verse says, and the side that bows is the heavier one. bowing shows weight.

practice: Bring to mind someone who once told you something true you didn't want to hear: a coach who corrected you, a friend who disagreed, maybe someone younger than you.
Remember what they said and how long it took you to see it, then lower your head a little, not to make yourself small, just to give the weight its due.
If you pray, give thanks for them; if you don't, hold them in mind with gratitude.

wordCard.voice: Humble before truth. The yogis honor the Word, not the winner; and in Guru Nanak's scale, the side that bows is the heavier one. Today's word.

orig.note: bows, bends low: from the Asa di Var verse where the side that bows is the heavier.

carryVoice: Your line: the yogis bowed. Sweetness and humility, mithat neevee, travel together. Rest well.
